nameStory: Sharp-leaved Fluellen gets its name from those distinctively pointed, sharp-edged leaves that help distinguish it from its rounder-leaved cousin. The name 'Fluellen' is quite old, possibly derived from the Welsh 'llysiau'r llew' meaning 'lion's herbs,' though the connection to lions remains a botanical mystery that adds to this little plant's charm.
description: Sharp-leaved Fluellen is a small, creeping annual plant that forms low mats along the ground. This European immigrant rarely grows more than a few inches tall but can spread outward in trailing stems up to a foot long. It produces tiny snapdragon-like flowers and has distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that give it its 'sharp-leaved' name. Despite being in the plantain family, it looks nothing like the common broad-leaved plantains most people know.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Arrow-shaped or triangular leaves with distinctly sharp, pointed tips and backward-pointing lobes at the base, feeling slightly fuzzy to the touch and arranged alternately along trailing stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny snapdragon-like flowers, usually yellow with a purple upper lip, about 1/4 inch long, sprouting singly from leaf joints on slender stalks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, trailing stems that creep along the ground forming small mats, never standing upright but spreading outward like a miniature groundcover

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules that split open to release tiny seeds, often persisting after flowers fade in late summer

habitat: Sharp-leaved Fluellen prefers disturbed soils in agricultural areas, particularly cultivated fields, gardens, and waste ground. It thrives in sandy or loamy soils and can often be found along field edges, in crop rows, or anywhere the soil has been recently turned over.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, with first leaves appearing as small rosettes in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from mid to late summer, with the tiny snapdragon-like blooms most visible during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open in early fall, releasing seeds before the plant dies with the first frost.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible; seeds overwinter in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Despite being extremely rare in New England with only 3 recorded sightings, Sharp-leaved Fluellen is considered a significant agricultural weed in parts of Europe, where it can reduce crop yields - making our few New England specimens botanical celebrities that somehow crossed the Atlantic!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Round-leaved Fluellen (its close relative) or small specimens of field bindweed, but the distinctive arrow-shaped leaves with sharp backward-pointing lobes are unique - remember 'sharp name, sharp leaves' as your identification key.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Kickxia honors Belgian botanist Jean Kickx, while 'Fluellen' appears in Shakespeare's Henry V as a character name, though whether the plant or character came first in English usage remains unclear to plant historians.
compareHints: Since Sharp-leaved Fluellen is the only Kickxia species recorded in New England, compare it to other small trailing members of the plantain family like speedwells (Veronica species). Unlike speedwells, Fluellen has distinctly arrow-shaped leaves and snapdragon-type flowers rather than the four-petaled, wheel-shaped flowers typical of speedwells.
